Progressive Jackpot Slots: How They Work and What "Must-Hit-By" Means

Published August 25, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Every progressive jackpot slot is really two games layered on top of each other: the ordinary spinning game with its own pay table and house edge, and a second, slower game where a growing pool of money waits for one specific trigger. Most players understand that the jackpot climbs the longer it goes unclaimed, but far fewer understand where that money is actually coming from, how it changes the math of the machine as it grows, or what a "must-hit-by" cap does to the odds. All three are worth knowing before you sit down at one.

In this guide

  1. What makes a jackpot "progressive"
  2. Standalone vs. local vs. wide-area progressives

What makes a jackpot "progressive"

A fixed-top-award slot pays the same maximum prize every time someone lands the top combination, and the pay table resets to that same number the next time it happens. A progressive slot instead sets aside a small slice of every wager placed on the game — and on wide-area versions, every wager placed on every linked machine across many casinos or sites — into a shared pool. That pool keeps growing, spin after spin, until it's won, at which point it drops back to a fixed starting amount called the seed and begins climbing again.

The contribution rate that funds the pool is usually a small fraction of each wager, built quietly into the game's overall design rather than disclosed as a specific line item to players. It's the reason progressive slots exist as a category at all: the base game funds a much larger, rarer prize than any single spin's bet size could otherwise support.

Standalone vs. local vs. wide-area progressives

Not all progressives grow the same way, and the difference matters for how quickly a jackpot builds and how large it can realistically get.

TypeFunded byTypical growth speed
StandaloneWagers on that one machine or one online game onlySlowest — smaller jackpots, but hit more often relative to size
Local / in-houseA group of machines linked within one casino or one operator's own siteFaster than standalone, still bounded by one operator's volume
Wide-area / networkMany machines linked across multiple casinos, states, or platformsFastest — capable of reaching the largest, headline-grabbing totals

Wide-area progressives are the ones responsible for the eye-catching totals you'll occasionally see reported, precisely because thousands of players across many properties are all feeding the same pool at once. That scale is also why wide-area games are usually the strictest about eligibility rules, which is covered below.

How the growing pool changes the game's math

A progressive slot's base-game RTP (return to player) is typically set lower than a comparable non-progressive slot, because a portion of every wager is being diverted into the jackpot pool instead of paying out through the regular pay table. Looked at in isolation, the base game is a slightly worse bet than a similar non-progressive machine. But the jackpot contribution is still part of the game's total theoretical return — it's just deferred and lumpy instead of paid out on every spin.

That has a real, if often overlooked, consequence: the game's combined theoretical RTP — base game plus jackpot — actually rises as the pool grows past its seed amount, and is mathematically at its best relative to long-run average right before a jackpot hits. The catch is that on a standard, uncapped progressive running on a random number generator, nobody can predict when that hit is coming — each qualifying spin is still an independent, memoryless event, and a jackpot sitting at ten times its seed is not statistically "closer" to hitting than one that just reset, unless the game specifically works differently, which is exactly what the next section covers. For more on how RTP works generally, see our guide to understanding RTP.

Worth remembering: a bigger pool means a bigger prize if you hit it, not better odds of hitting it — unless the specific game you're playing is designed with a hard ceiling, which changes the math in a real and provable way.

What "must-hit-by" actually means

A small but growing category of progressive games — often marketed as "must-hit-by," "mystery," or similarly named jackpots — build in an actual guarantee: the jackpot is programmed to pay out by the time the pool reaches a stated ceiling, for example a jackpot that must hit before the pool climbs past a posted cap. Unlike a standard uncapped progressive, where the odds of triggering the jackpot stay statistically constant no matter how large the pool gets, a must-hit-by game's internal trigger logic pushes the probability of a hit upward as the pool approaches that ceiling, since the game mathematically cannot let the pool exceed the stated number without paying out first.

This is a real, specific mechanic that only applies to games explicitly designed and marketed that way — it's disclosed in the game's rules or paytable screen, not something you can assume applies to any progressive you happen to be playing. The large majority of classic progressive jackpots, including most wide-area ones, have no ceiling at all and could in theory run indefinitely without ever forcing a hit.

A simple worked example

To see the difference, picture two hypothetical versions of the same game side by side. Both seed at $10,000 after a win and grow at roughly the same pace as players wager on them. The standard uncapped version happens to run all the way up to $85,000 before someone hits it — a large number, but nothing about the odds changed along the way; every spin from $10,001 to $85,000 carried the same underlying probability of triggering the jackpot. A must-hit-by version of the same game, capped at $75,000, would have been mathematically guaranteed to pay out before ever reaching that $85,000 mark — meaning its trigger probability was already climbing well before the pool got anywhere close to the ceiling, purely because of how the game is built, not because of any pattern in the spins themselves.

This example is illustrative rather than drawn from any specific casino's real numbers, but the underlying mechanic — a rising trigger probability as a capped pool approaches its ceiling, versus a flat trigger probability on an uncapped pool — is exactly how the two game types actually differ.

Practical things to check before you play

Many progressive games require a maximum or specific qualifying bet size to be eligible for the full top jackpot; some pay a smaller, secondary jackpot tier to players betting below that level, and a few exclude non-max bettors from the top prize entirely. That eligibility detail is almost always disclosed on the game's rules or paytable screen, and it's worth checking before you start playing, since it directly affects whether your actual bet size even has a shot at the number displayed on the meter.

It's also worth being clear-eyed about bankroll math: chasing a large progressive on a game with a below-average base RTP means accepting worse odds on the vast majority of spins in exchange for a rare shot at a large prize, which is a legitimate way to play but a different trade than picking a game purely for its long-run return. And the common myth that a jackpot is "due" because it hasn't hit in a while only holds any truth for the specific, disclosed must-hit-by style of game described above — on every other progressive, a pool that's been growing for months is not, on its own, any more likely to hit on the next spin than it was the day it reset. For more on how volatility and bankroll interact more broadly, see our slot volatility guide.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to bet the maximum to win a progressive jackpot?

It depends on the specific game. Some require a maximum or qualifying bet size for eligibility on the top jackpot tier, sometimes offering a smaller consolation jackpot to other bettors; the rules screen for each game discloses this.

What happens to the jackpot pool right after someone wins it?

It resets to a fixed starting amount called the seed, and the pool begins accumulating again from that base as future wagers contribute to it.

Are progressive slots always a worse bet than regular slots?

The base game typically carries a lower RTP than a comparable non-progressive slot, since part of every wager funds the jackpot pool. Whether that's a "worse bet" depends on how you weigh a lower average return against a rare shot at a much larger prize.

What does "must-hit-by" actually guarantee?

It guarantees the jackpot will pay out before the pool reaches a stated ceiling, and only on games specifically designed and marketed with that mechanic. It doesn't apply to standard uncapped progressives, where the odds of hitting stay constant regardless of pool size.

Can a wide-area jackpot be won by two different players close together?

Yes, in principle — since a wide-area jackpot is shared across many machines and players simultaneously, the pool resets the moment any one player triggers it, regardless of who else happened to be playing the same network at that time.
